content:
It's not uncommon to see files of this form

theorem a (h : stuff) : ... := by ...
theorem b (h : stuff) : ... := by ...
theorem c (h : stuff) : ... := by ...
theorem d (h : stuff) : ... := by ...

where it could have been like

variable (h : stuff)
include h

theorem a : ... := by ...
theorem b : ... := by ...
theorem c : ... := by ...
theorem d : ... := by ...

Of course this is to be applied with discretion, since variable can make it confusing where the hypothesis come from. But I think in cases where every theorem or definition in the file uses the variable/hypothesis, this is pretty justified.

Thought about making this into either a lint rule or a review rubric? (Problem with lint rule is sometimes you want to make exceptions...?)

Mathlib precedent: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/aa4180fd65f90dd50307a354941dfbee635cf9d2/Mathlib/FieldTheory/KummerExtension.lean#L174 (although this case has include ... in for each theorem instead of over the whole section)
For implicit conditions, I very much agree. For explicit ones, I'm less convinced. This can make it harder to see what's going on in the actual theorem statement.

• How do you distinguish between implicit and explicit condition?
  • If AI reviewers are good enough at it, we can still make it a rubric. Although enough here means better than random guess. (But some mechanism needs to be in place to prevent flip-flop.)

In variable (h : stuff), the argument h is explicit: the parentheses are explicit binders.
In variable {h : stuff}, the argument h is implicit, because of the parentheses { } uses.

Fortunately this should be mechanically lintable, unfortunately AI doesn't seem too good at determining whether a variable should be explicit or implicit either.

(I'd guess apart from semantic, one prefer to make variables implicit if they can be deduced almost all the time, but the AI will happily add @ or (name := value).)

There are two questions here, and I'm not sure if you're confusing those:
(1) should a given hypothesis/parameter be explicit or implicit
(2) should a given hypothesis be extracted into a variable command

You don't need to have answers to (1) to think about (2)!

It's good to have some rubric, but maybe a lint rule would be too strong. What happens if you have an implicit argument (which you'd move to a variable) after an explicit argument (which is arguably clearer if put in the theorem statement)?

David Ang said:

It's good to have some rubric, but maybe a lint rule would be too strong. What happens if you have an implicit argument (which you'd move to a variable) after an explicit argument (which is arguably clearer if put in the theorem statement)?

I imagine in this case it's fine to reorder them?
